messages.author: 2c868cf345b264e6
messages.subject: Angle measurement and crabbing
parts:
Dear List

In ship-board cetacean surveys there seem to be two main methods in =
common
use for measuring the angle or bearing of a sighting, which is required =
in
order
to calculate the distance of the sighting from the trackline. Some =
workers
use a compass to measure a bearing to the sighting, while others use an
angle board to measure the angle of the sighting relative to the heading
of the vessel.

The use of angle boards assumes that the vessel is heading along the =
axis
of the trackline. However, this is frequently not the case. Currents =
flowing
across the trackline cause the vessel to head somewhat into the =
direction
the current is coming from in order to follow a pre-determined course or
trackline, in which case the vessel is not aligned with the trackline. =
This
is known as crabbing. Lateral winds may also cause a vessel to crab. In
these circumstances, angles measured with a sightings board that is =
aligned
with the axis of the vessel will be inaccurate.

Crabbing angles vary with the strength of currents and their angle in
relation
to the trackline. Thus on a given survey day, the crabbing angle will =
change
as currents change (tidal currents are not constant but ebb and flow) =
and
with changes in trackline direction.

The situation is likely to be even worse in the case of small survey =
vessels
that may weave about from side to side in order to follow a trackline,
whereas
larger vessels using an autopilot generally settle down to a constant
crabbing
angle.

After some discussion with colleagues, two points of view have emerged =
about
this problem:

1) It does not matter because sightings are distributed randomly on =
either
side of the trackline.

2) It does matter because the potential inaccuracy can be quite large =
(of
the order of 10 degrees) and if we take care to make our distance
estimations
as accurate as possible then we should do the same for our angle =
estimates.

Angle boards are cheap to implement and simple to use. But should we be
using them for Distance sampling unless we also record the actual =
heading
of the vessel at the time angles are measured?

Mick Baines
Sea Watch Foundation
UK

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Angle measurement and crabbing
parts:
Mark, the problem of crabbing tends to be more severe in aerial surveys,
especially helicopters. In practice, I think this is seldom a major
problem with ship surveys, though it may be for small boats. The real
advantage that angle boards bring is the avoidance of angles rounded to
zero degrees. Error in the angles will lead to some bias in estimating
the detection function, but bias in estimating abundance should be very
small. By contrast, rounding to zero degrees can generate substantial
bias in the abundance estimate. It might be interesting to conduct a
simulation study to see just how large the error needs to be before it
really matters.

Some survey lasers automatically give angles relative to the
transect line. Lasers tend not to be used in marine surveys, because you
can't use them to measure distances to points on water, but I've often
thought that they might still be very useful for improving accuracy of
angle estimation. Does anyone use them for this purpose? If so, how
effective are they?

Steve Buckland
